title: Why unfinished tasks refuse to leave
text: It was the Russian psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik {{1}} first noticed that waiters remembered orders perfectly {{2}} the bill was settled — and forgot them immediately afterwards. Decades of research have confirmed the pattern: we recall unfinished tasks {{3}} accurately than finished ones, and an interrupted essay will nag at its author {{4}} it is done. The modern version of the effect is the unread counter on your phone, engineered {{5}} exploit {{6}} psychologists call open loops: the mind keeps circling back to anything left hanging. {{7}} writing tomorrow's list before leaving the desk is not fussy bureaucracy but a way of telling your brain the loop is closed — that the next step is safely recorded somewhere {{8}} than in working memory.

gaps.explanation: Cleft-supporting relative about a person: who.

gaps.hint: time word: remembered orders ___ the bill was settled
gaps.explanation: 'Until' marks the end of the remembering.
'More accurately than' — the first element of the comparison is gapped.

gaps.hint: time word: will nag ___ it is done
gaps.explanation: The nagging continues up to completion: until.
'Engineered to exploit' — the infinitive of purpose.

gaps.hint: pronoun: exploit ___ psychologists call open loops
gaps.explanation: Fused relative object: what psychologists call.
'By + gerund' — the means of closing the loop.
'Other than' — the fixed phrase of exception.
